source_text: Τῶν μὲν οὖν προγεγενημένων θεὸς δίδωσιν ἄφεσιν. τῶν δὲ ἐπιόντων αὐτὸς ἕκαστος ἑαυτῷ. καὶ τοῦτ᾿ ἔστι μεταγνῶναι τὸ καταγνῶναι τῶν παρῳχημένων καὶ αἰτήσασθαι τούτων ἀμνηστίαν παρὰ πατρός, ὃς μόνος τῶν ἁπάντων οἷός τέ ἐστιν ἄπρακτα ποιῆσαι τὰ πεπραγμένα ἐλέῳ τῷ παρ᾿ αὑτοῦ καὶ δρόσῳ πνεύματος ἀπαλείψας τὰ προημαρτημένα. »ἐφ᾿ οἷς γὰρ ἂν εὕρω ὑμᾶς«, φησίν, »ἐπὶ τούτοις καὶ κρινῶ·« καὶ παρ᾿ ἕκαστα βοᾷ τὸ τέλος πάντων· ὥστε καὶ τῷ τὰ μέγιστα εὖ πεποιηκότι κατὰ τὸν βίον, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ τέλους ἐξοκείλαντι πρὸς κακίαν, ἀνόνητοι πάντες οἱ πρόσθεν πόνοι, ἐπὶ τῆς καταστροφῆς τοῦ δράματος ἐξάθλῳ γενομένῳ, τῷ τε χεῖρον καὶ ἐπισεσυρμένως βιώσαντι πρότερον ἔστιν ὕστερον μετανοήσαντι πολλοῦ χρόνου πολιτείαν πονηρὰν ἐκνικῆσαι τῷ μετὰ τὴν μετάνοιαν χρόνῳ· ἀκριβείας δὲ δεῖ πολλῆς, ὥσπερ τοῖς μακρᾷ νόσῳ πεπονηκόσι σώμασι διαίτης χρεία καὶ προσοχῆς πλείονος. ὁ κλέπτης, ἄφεσιν βούλει λαβεῖν; μηκέτι κλέπτε· ὁ μοιχεύσας, μηκέτι πυρούσθω· ὁ πορνεύσας, λοιπὸν ἁγνευέτω· ὁ ἁρπάσας, ἀποδίδου καὶ προσαποδίδου· ὁ ψευδομάρτυς. ἀλήθειαν ἄσκησον· ὁ ἐπίορκος, μηκέτι ὄμνυε· καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάθη σύντεμε, ὀργήν, ἐπιθυμίαν, λύπην. φόβον, ἵνα εὑρεθῇς ἐπὶ τῆς ἐξόδου πρὸς τὸν ἀντίδικον ἐνταῦθα διαλελύσθαι φθάνων. ἔστιν μὲν οὖν ἀδύνατον ἴσως ἀθρόως ἀποκόψαι πάθη σύντροφα, ἀλλὰ μετὰ θεοῦ δυνάμεως καὶ ἀνθρωπείας ἱκεσίας καὶ ἀδελφῶν βοηθείας καὶ εἰλικρινοῦς μετανοίας καὶ συνεχοῦς μελέτης κατορθοῦται.
thought_title: Forgiveness for the past, repentance for the future
orientation: Clement is addressing his readers directly, explaining what true repentance requires after having shown that God patiently waits for those who turn.
pass_a_gloss: Of the things that have already happened, God gives forgiveness. But of the things that are coming, each person himself gives it to himself. And this is to repent: to condemn the things that are past and to ask for forgetfulness of them from the Father, who alone of all beings is able to make the things that have been done undone, by the mercy that comes from himself and by the dew of the Spirit, wiping away the sins committed before. "For in whatever things I find you," he says, "in those things also I will judge you"; and at each point the end of all things cries out. So that even for the one who has done the greatest good deeds throughout his life, but at the end has run aground toward wickedness, all his former labors are without profit, since at the catastrophe of the drama he has become utterly wretched; and for the one who has lived worse and more carelessly before, it is possible, if he repents later, to overcome a wicked way of life of much time by the time after repentance. But much precision is needed, just as for bodies that have suffered from a long illness there is need of a regimen and of greater attention. You who steal, do you wish to receive forgiveness? Steal no longer. You who have committed adultery, burn no longer. You who have fornicated, be pure from now on. You who have robbed, give back and give back more. You who bear false witness, practice truth. You who swear falsely, swear no longer. And cut short the other passions: anger, desire, grief, fear, so that you may be found at your departure to have already been released from your adversary here. It is perhaps impossible to cut off at once passions that have grown up with one, but with the power of God and human supplication and the help of brothers and sincere repentance and constant practice it is accomplished.

lemmas.gloss: having run aground, drifted off course

choices.english: to make the things that have been done undone
choices.why: Preserves the paradox of the Greek: God alone can render accomplished deeds without effect, which is the point of Clement's argument about forgiveness.
rejected: to nullify what has been done

choices.english: at the catastrophe of the drama
choices.why: Keeps the theatrical metaphor Clement uses for the end of life, where the final act reveals the whole.
rejected: at the final scene of the play
at the end of the drama

choices.why: The adverb suggests a life dragged along without deliberate effort, which fits Clement's contrast with the one who did great good deeds.
rejected: has lived in a slipshod way

choices.why: The imperative means to prune or cut down, matching the agricultural metaphor of cutting off passions.
The participle φθάνων with the perfect infinitive conveys arriving at the point of departure already having settled the case, which is Clement's point about resolving matters before death.
rejected: to have gotten ahead in being released

pass_b_english: For the things that have already happened, God grants forgiveness; for the things that are still to come, each person grants it to himself. And this is what it means to repent: to condemn what is past and to ask the Father for pardon of these things. He alone of all beings is able to make the things that have been done undone, wiping away former sins by the mercy that comes from Him and by the dew of the Spirit. "For in whatever I find you," He says, "in that I will also judge you," and at every turn He proclaims the end of all things. So even for the one who has done the greatest good deeds throughout his life, if at the end he has run aground on wickedness, all his former labors are useless, since he has become utterly wretched at the catastrophe of the drama. But for the one who has lived more carelessly and badly before, it is possible later, by repenting, to overcome a long time of wicked conduct by the time that follows repentance. Yet great precision is needed, just as bodies that have suffered from a long illness need a regimen and greater attention. You who steal, do you want to receive forgiveness? Steal no longer. You who have committed adultery, burn no longer. You who have fornicated, be pure from now on. You who have seized what belongs to others, give it back and give back more besides. You who have borne false witness, practice the truth. You who have sworn falsely, swear no more. And cut short the other passions as well—anger, desire, grief, fear—so that at your departure you may be found to have already settled with your adversary here. It is perhaps impossible to cut off at once passions that have grown up with us, but with the power of God and human supplication and the help of brothers and sisters and sincere repentance and constant practice, it is accomplished.

problems.quote: "For in whatever I find you," He says, "in that I will also judge you" (Matthew 7:2)
problems.source_quote: ἐφ᾿ οἷς γὰρ ἂν εὕρω ὑμᾶς, φησίν, ἐπὶ τούτοις καὶ κρινῶ
problems.why: Matthew 7:2 is about measure-for-measure judgment, not this quote. This is an apocryphal/patristic saying.
problems.fix: Remove the incorrect reference or replace with a note that this is a non-canonical saying.
problems.ruling: Greek quote not from Matthew 7:2; misattributed scripture misleads reader

problems.quote: to ask the Father for forgetfulness of these things
problems.why: Greek says ask the Father for a pardon (amnesty), not forgetfulness.
problems.fix: to ask the Father for pardon of these things
problems.ruling: ἀμνηστίαν means amnesty/pardon, not forgetfulness; rendering changes meaning and misleads reader.

problems.source_quote: ἵνα εὑρεθῇς ἐπὶ τῆς ἐξόδου πρὸς τὸν ἀντίδικον ἐνταῦθα διαλελύσθαι φθάνων
problems.why: Source means 'so that at your departure you may be found to have already settled with your adversary here.' 'Released from' misreads διαλελύσθαι.
problems.fix: so that at your departure you may be found to have already settled with your adversary here
problems.ruling: Greek διαλελύσθαι (perfect passive) means ‘to have been dissolved/settled (a dispute)’, not ‘released from’; alters meaning of phrase.

edits.old: so that at your departure you may be found to have already been released from your adversary here
edits.new: so that at your departure you may be found to have already settled with your adversary here

fixed: Changed 'released from' to 'settled with' to match διαλελύσθαι, which means to have settled or been reconciled with one's adversary, not to be released from them.

last_rejected.why: Greek says ‘to know the condemnation of the sins’, not ‘to condemn’ them.
last_rejected.fix: to recognize the condemnation of the sins that have been committed
last_rejected.ruling: καταγνῶναι means 'condemn'; μεταγνῶναι τὸ καταγνῶναι = 'to repent is to condemn.' Claimed reading is unsupported.

last_rejected.why: Greek means ‘let him no longer be burned (punished)’, not that the adulterer should stop burning.
last_rejected.fix: let him no longer be burned
last_rejected.ruling: πυρούσθω is passive of πυρόω, 'be inflamed/burned with passion.' 'Burn no longer' correctly renders the passive imperative.

last_rejected.quote: so that at your departure you may be found to have already settled with your adversary here
last_rejected.source_quote: ἵνα εὑρεθῇς ἐπὶ τῆς ἐξόδου πρὸς τὸν ἀντίδικον ἐνταῦθα διαλελύσθαι φθάνων
last_rejected.why: Greek says ‘so that you may be found, at the departure, before the adversary, having been judged as a criminal’, not ‘settled with your adversary’. The sense changes from judgment to reconciliation.

last_rejected.ruling: διαλελύσθαι from διαλύω means 'be released/settled'; φθάνων with participle = 'having already.' 'Settled' is valid, not 'judged as criminal.'
